title: 1957 AHSME Problem 24
statement: If the square of a number of two digits is decreased by the square of the number formed by reversing the digits, then the result is not always divisible by:

solutions.text:
If the digits are \(a,b,\) then \[ \begin{aligned} &(10a+b)^2-(10b+a)^2\\ &\quad=[9(a-b)][11(a+b)]\\ &\quad=99(a-b)(a+b). \end{aligned} \] This is always divisible by \(9,\) \(11,\) the digit sum, and the digit difference. It need not be divisible by the digit product; for example, \(21^2-12^2=297\) is not divisible by \(2.\)

Thus, the correct answer is B.
hints: Represent the number as \(10a+b\) and its reversal as \(10b+a\)
Factor the difference of their squares completely
